passages.title: Nūḥ sent as a warner to his people
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat open the surah with a commission and its immediate answer. Allah tells us that He sent Nūḥ (peace be upon him) to his people with one instruction — warn them before a painful torment reaches them — and Nūḥ turns to them and delivers exactly that, naming what they must do and what they will gain by it. The passage runs as a single unbroken line: Allah sends, the messenger warns, he names three demands, he names two promises, and he closes with the reminder that the term appointed by Allah, once it arrives, is not postponed.

## A warning that arrives while there is still time

Ibn Kathir sums up the sending in a way that colours everything after it. Allah sent Nūḥ to his people **commanding him to warn them of the punishment of Allah before it befell them**, and he was to tell them that **if they would repent and turn to Allah, then the punishment would be lifted from them.**

Read that carefully. On Ibn Kathir's reading, the warning is not the punishment beginning. It is the punishment still held back, with a way out named out loud. The force of the ayah sits in the words *min qabli an ya'tiyahum* — "**before** there comes to them a painful torment." Time is still open. A warner has arrived, and with him an offer: repent, turn to Allah, and what was coming is lifted.

This is worth pausing on, because people instinctively hear warning as hostility. Here it is the opposite: the one who tells you the roof is about to fall is the one who wants you out from under it. And notice that Nūḥ is not sent with the bad news only. He is sent with the bad news *and the remedy*, in the same breath.

## "A plain warner"

Nūḥ's answer opens with the words *yā qawmi* — **"O my people! Verily, I am a plain warner to you."**

Ibn Kathir glosses that phrase as **"clarity of the warning, making the matter apparent and clear."** So the claim Nūḥ makes for himself is a claim about clarity. He is not merely saying that he means well; he is saying that the matter is being set before them plainly — apparent and clear, not veiled, not left in a shape that could later be pleaded as a misunderstanding.

That is itself part of the mercy. When Allah decides to warn a people, He does not warn them obscurely.

## Three demands

*"That you should worship Allah, and have Taqwā of Him, and obey me."* Ibn Kathir takes the first two together, and the third on its own.

**"Worship Allah, and have Taqwā of Him"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as *"abandon those things that He has forbidden and avoid that which He has declared to be sinful."*

This is a gift to anyone who has struggled with the word *taqwā*, which is often translated vaguely as "fear" or "consciousness of Allah" and then left floating as a mood. Ibn Kathir gives it hands and feet. In this ayah it is measured in what you leave: you identify what Allah has forbidden, and you stop.

**"And obey me"** — Ibn Kathir: *"In that which I command you to do and that which I forbid you from."*

Notice that the obedience being asked for has a defined content. It is not attachment to a personality; it is bounded by what the messenger actually commands and actually forbids. And when Ibn Kathir reaches the promise in the next ayah, he holds the same two things together: *"if you do what I command you to do and you believe in what I have been sent with to you, then Allah will forgive you for your sins."* Doing and believing are both named there.

## Two promises

*"He will forgive you of your sins and respite you to an appointed term."*

### The small word *min*

Maarif ul Quran opens this phrase carefully. The Arabic reads *yaghfir lakum **min** dhunūbikum* — "He will forgive you **of** your sins."

The commentary notes that the particle *min* is often used **to indicate division into parts** — that is, to refer to only a part of an amount, group or number. If it is taken in that sense here, it would signify that by embracing the faith, only those sins would be forgiven which pertain to the **Divine rights**. Violation of **human rights** would be forgiven only when the believer fulfils the human rights he has violated — such as pecuniary obligations, meaning what he owes financially — and if they cannot be fulfilled — such as having hurt somebody physically or verbally — then **the person who has been so hurt must first be requested to forgive.**

Maarif ul Quran then adds something important: the hadith which reports that by embracing the faith all sins are forgiven **must be understood in the light of that explanation**. In other words, that hadith carries the same conditions as this verse: violation of the rights of human beings is not forgiven except upon fulfilment of those rights, or seeking forgiveness from the victims of that violation. (The commentary refers to this hadith without naming a collection, so it is passed on here exactly as it is given there, and no further.)

**Where the scholars differed:** Maarif ul Quran reports that other scholars of tafsir interpret *min* here as *zā'idah* — "extra," having no meaning of its own and added only because of usage — in which way the verse signifies that **all** their sins would be forgiven. Even on that reading, the commentary adds, on the basis of other texts this general expression is subject to the conditions mentioned above.

This is one of the most practically weighty points in the passage. A person can turn to Allah tonight in tears and be forgiven — and still owe his brother the money, still owe his sister the apology.

### "And respite you to an appointed term"

Ibn Kathir's gloss: *"He will extend your life span and protect you from the torment that He would have made befall you if you did not stay away from His prohibitions."* Two things are promised at once — added life, and shelter from the torment that would otherwise have come.

Ibn Kathir notes that **this ayah is used as proof by those who say that obedience to Allah, righteousness, and maintaining the family ties truly increase the life span of a person.** He connects it to what has been reported in the Hadith: **"Maintaining the family ties increases the life span."** (Ibn Kathir gives this without naming a collection, so it is passed on here as he gives it, with no collection attached.)

That is a striking thing to sit with. The passage is about a nation facing destruction — and among the things named as lengthening a life is something as domestic as keeping up with your relatives.

### "Verily, the term of Allah when it comes, cannot be delayed"

The second half of the ayah closes the door that the first half seemed to leave open. Ibn Kathir reads it as urgency: **hasten to the obedience of Allah before the coming of His vengeance.** For if He commands that to happen, **it cannot be repulsed or prevented** — *"For He is the Great One Who compels everything, and He is the Almighty Whose might all of creation succumbs to."*

Those closing words of Ibn Kathir are a description of Allah as He has described Himself: greatness before which everything yields, might to which all of creation submits. We affirm that as it came, without likening it to anything in creation and without emptying it of its meaning.

Hold the two halves of the ayah together and the logic is exact. Yes, there is respite — and the respite has a ceiling, and the ceiling is fixed.

And then the closing words, *law kuntum taʿlamūn* — **"if you but know."** Ibn Kathir turns the sentence into a summons rather than a lament: hasten, before the vengeance comes. The matter has been made apparent and clear. What remains is whether anyone acts on what has been made clear to them.

## Living it

Ibn Kathir's reading of this passage turns it directly on the reader:

- **Treat a warning as a mercy in progress.** On Ibn Kathir's reading, Nūḥ was sent to warn *before* the punishment came — and to say that repentance and turning to Allah would lift it.
- **Make taqwā concrete.** Ibn Kathir's explanation is a to-do list, not a mood: abandon what Allah has forbidden, avoid what He has declared sinful.
- **Settle what you owe people.** Maarif ul Quran is explicit: rights owed to other human beings are met by fulfilling them, or by asking the one you wronged to forgive.
- **Keep your family ties.** Ibn Kathir places this among the things said to increase a person's life span, alongside obedience and righteousness.
- **Do not schedule your obedience.** Ibn Kathir's instruction is to hasten — because the term appointed by Allah, when it comes, cannot be delayed.

The passage ends where it began: a warning delivered plainly while there is still time, a way out named in the same breath, and a term that will not be pushed back once it arrives.

passages.title: Nūḥ complains of centuries of fruitless calling
passages.tafsir:
**In these five ayat the surah hands the microphone to Nuh himself.** Ibn Kathir opens the passage by telling us what is happening: Allah is telling us about His servant and Messenger, Nuh (peace be upon him), and how he complained to his Lord about the response he received from his people. So what we are hearing is the messenger's own report, spoken not to an audience but to his Lord: *"My Lord! I have surely called my people day and night…"* (ayah 5). What binds ayat 5–9 into one unit is that they are a single sustained complaint, and every line in it does one of two things — it describes how relentlessly he called (ayat 5, 8, 9), or how completely they refused (ayat 6, 7).

## A grievance carried to the only One worth telling

Ibn Kathir adds two details that set the scale of what we are reading. First, the length of it: Nuh was patient with these people for a long period of time, which he gives as nine hundred and fifty years. Second, the cause of the complaint: it came, Ibn Kathir says, from his explaining and clarifying matters for them and his calling them to guidance and the straightest path. In other words, this is not the complaint of a man who did too little. It is the complaint of a man who did everything, for nearly a millennium, and watched it come to nothing.

Notice, too, where the complaint goes. Nuh does not vent to a sympathetic follower or curse his people from a hilltop. He turns to Allah and begins with a single word: **رَبِّ (Rabbi)** — "my Lord," with the possessive attached. The whole grievance is spoken inside a relationship, addressed to the One who had sent him.

## Ayah 5 — "night and day"

**دَعَوْتُ قَوْمِي لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا** — "I called my people, night and day."

Ibn Kathir reads the line as Nuh saying: *I did not abandon calling them night and day, carrying out Your command and in obedience to You.*

That last phrase is the hinge of the entire complaint. Nuh is not reporting a personal project that failed. He is reporting on an assignment, to the One who assigned it. His calling was itself obedience — an act of worship discharged whether or not anyone answered. Hold that next to the nine hundred and fifty years, and "night and day" stops sounding like a flourish. It is a summary of a lifetime of walking into the same rejection.

## Ayah 6 — the only thing that increased

**فَلَمْ يَزِدْهُمْ دُعَائِي إِلَّا فِرَارًا** — literally, "so my calling increased them in nothing but flight."

Feel the bitter arithmetic of that sentence. Nuh's calling *did* produce an increase — it simply produced the opposite one. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: the more he called them to come to the truth, the more they fled from it and avoided it. Every fresh invitation added distance instead of closing it.

They were not staying to weigh the message and finding it wanting. In Ibn Kathir's words they *fled from it and avoided it* — a movement away, not an argument back.

## Ayah 7 — a portrait of refusal

Ayah 7 is the heart of the passage, and it is filmed in close-up.

**"Every time I called unto them."** Not "when I called them" — *every* time. Their refusal was not a bad day; it was the fixed response, repeated as often as the invitation was.

**لِتَغْفِرَ لَهُمْ — "that You might forgive them."** Look carefully at what Nuh tells his Lord he was calling them *for*. Not so they would respect him, or accept his leadership, or admit that he had been right for centuries. So that *Allah* would forgive *them*. The whole aim of the call was a benefit that would land on the people who were refusing him. That is the temperament of a prophet.

**They thrust their fingers into their ears.** Ibn Kathir explains it exactly as it sounds: they closed up their ears so that they could not hear what he was calling them to. And he draws a striking parallel — this is what Allah records of the disbelievers of the Quraysh, who said to one another, *"Listen not to this Qur'an, and make noise in the midst of its recitation, that you may overcome"* (41:26). Two peoples separated by ages, reaching for the same defence, because the danger was the same: the message might get in.

**They covered themselves with their garments (وَاسْتَغْشَوْا ثِيَابَهُمْ).** Here the early scholars offer two readings, and Ibn Kathir preserves both rather than declaring one final:

- Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that they concealed themselves under false pretences from him, so that he would not recognise them.
- Sa'id bin Jubayr and As-Suddi both said that they covered their heads so that they could not hear what he was saying — the garment as soundproofing, doubling the work their fingers were already doing.

Either way the picture is the same: a person actively arranging their own deafness. And notice the effort involved. It takes far more work to plug your ears and pull a cloak over your head than simply to listen and disagree.

**وَأَصَرُّوا — "and they persisted."** Ibn Kathir: they continued in what they were already upon of associating partners with Allah and great disbelief. Not a fresh sin, then, but the old one held on to — the refusal renewed each time the call came.

**وَاسْتَكْبَرُوا اسْتِكْبَارًا — "and they magnified themselves in pride."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and worth memorising, because it tells you what pride actually *does*: it means they were turned away from following the truth and submitting to it.

That names the real obstacle. Their problem was never a shortage of clarity — Ibn Kathir has already told us Nuh spent those centuries explaining and clarifying matters for them. The obstacle was **istikbār**, self-magnification, and what it produced was precisely a turning away from following the truth and submitting to it. Fingers in the ears are only ever the symptom.

## Ayat 8–9 — a man trying every door

Having described the refusal, Nuh returns to his own effort — and the last two ayat of our passage are essentially an inventory of methods.

**ثُمَّ إِنِّي دَعَوْتُهُمْ جِهَارًا** (ayah 8) — "then I called them **openly**." Ibn Kathir: openly, among the people.

**ثُمَّ إِنِّي أَعْلَنتُ لَهُمْ** (ayah 9) — "then I proclaimed to them **publicly**." Ibn Kathir distinguishes it: with open speech and a raised voice.

**وَأَسْرَرْتُ لَهُمْ إِسْرَارًا** — "and I appealed to them **privately**." Ibn Kathir: in discussions with them. The crowd was not the only place he tried; he also sat with them and talked.

Ibn Kathir sums up the whole sequence in one sentence: *he tried various types of propagation to be more effective with them.* That is the point of the ladder — the timing (night and day), the openness, the raised voice, and then the quiet conversation. Nuh exhausted the possibilities. He changed his method again and again without ever changing his message once.

And notice what he never once claims. He never says he made anyone believe. He reports his effort, in detail, and the outcome, honestly — and leaves the verdict where it belongs.

## Living it

**Your job is the calling, not the converting.** Ibn Kathir has Nuh describing his work as carrying out Allah's command and obedience to Him. Nine hundred and fifty years of it, and the tally in ayah 6 is a negative number. If that is not counted as failure, then neither is your unanswered advice to a relative, your unread message, your years of quiet example. The deed was complete when you did it.

**Vary the method, never the message.** Ayat 8–9 give you the range: open and private, the raised voice and the sitting-down conversation. Ibn Kathir's summary is the instruction — try various kinds of calling in order to be more effective. When one door is shut, try another door to the same house.

**Aim at their forgiveness, not your vindication.** Ayah 7's *"that You might forgive them"* is the corrective for every argument we have ever won while losing the person in the process.

**Take the complaint to Allah.** Nuh's exhaustion is real and it is in the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir does not soften it; he says outright that Nuh complained to his Lord. Nuh does not pretend to be untired. He simply brings it to the right address, and begins with *Rabbi* — "my Lord."

**And watch for the fingers in your own ears.** Every one of us has a subject we would rather not hear a reminder about, and a way of arranging our life so that we don't. Ibn Kathir's diagnosis is worth keeping close: underneath the stopped ears and the covered heads was self-magnification — and what it amounted to, in the end, was being turned away from following the truth and submitting to it.

passages.title: Seek forgiveness and He will pour blessings
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** after nine and a half centuries of preaching, Nuh (peace be upon him) tells his Lord what he actually said to his people — and it comes down to a single command, *"Ask forgiveness from your Lord,"* followed by a chain of promises: rain, wealth, children, gardens, rivers. One door, and everything Nuh says opens behind it.

## Where these ayat sit

These three ayat are not Allah speaking directly to us. They are Nuh quoting himself inside a complaint he is making to his Lord. Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Allah "tells about His servant and Messenger, Nuh, and that he complained to his Lord about the response he received from his people, and how he was patient with them for this long period of time — which was nine hundred and fifty years."

Read what comes just before, and ayah 10 lands with far more weight:

- **Ayah 5** — "I have called to my people night and day." Ibn Kathir glosses this as: *I did not abandon calling them night and day, carrying out Your command and in obedience to You.*
- **Ayah 6** — his calling only increased their flight. The more he called them to come to the truth, the more they fled from it and avoided it.
- **Ayah 7** — fingers in ears, garments pulled over themselves. Ibn Kathir: they closed up their ears so they could not hear what he was calling them to — and he notes the same reflex in the disbelievers of Quraysh, who told each other not to listen to the Qur'an and to make noise over its recitation (41:26). On the garments, Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas that "they concealed themselves under false pretences from him so that he would not recognize them"; Saʿid bin Jubayr and As-Suddi both said, "They covered their heads so that they could not hear what he was saying." And they *persisted* — Ibn Kathir: they continued in what they were upon of associating partners with Allah (shirk) and great disbelief — and *magnified themselves in pride*, meaning they were turned away from following the truth and submitting to it.
- **Ayat 8–9** — so he varied his method: openly among the people, then in public with open speech and a raised voice, then privately in discussion with them. Ibn Kathir's summary: "he tried various types of propagation to be more effective with them."

Then ayah 10 opens with **fa-qultu** — "so I said." After all that effort and all those centuries, this is the content. Not a new argument. The same invitation, put in its simplest form.

## Ayah 10: the command, and the name it rests on

**"I said: Ask forgiveness from your Lord, verily, He is Oft-Forgiving."**

Ibn Kathir's paraphrase of the command is worth sitting with: *"return to Him and turn away from what you are involved in. Repent to Him soon."*

Three things are packed into that.

**One — it is a turn, not just a phrase.** "Ask forgiveness" here means turning back *and* turning away: leaving what you are currently involved in. Nuh is not handing his people a formula to recite while their lives stay the same.

**Two — do it soon.** Ibn Kathir adds the word deliberately: *repent to Him soon*. Said to a people who had been called for centuries, it is a warning wrapped in an invitation.

**Three — nothing is too big.** Nuh anchors the command in a name of Allah: **Ghaffār**, which Ibn Kathir's text renders "Oft-Forgiving." He explains: "verily, He is Most Accepting of the repentance of those who turn to Him in repentance. He will accept repentance no matter what the sin is, **even if it is disbelief and polytheism**."

That last clause is the hinge of the whole passage. Ayah 7 has just told us exactly what these people were guilty of — associating partners with Allah, and "great disbelief." And ayah 10 tells them that this — precisely this — is forgivable if they turn. Nuh does not soften what they had done; he tells them the door is open anyway. And he does not send them to a stranger: the ayah says *"your Lord."*

## Ayat 11–12: what Nuh says follows

Ibn Kathir makes the link explicit. He does not read the promises as a separate topic; he reads them as the answer to the command, and states the condition in so many words — *"if you repent to Allah, seek His forgiveness and obey Him, He will increase your provisions for you…"* Ask, and this follows.

### Rain that keeps coming (ayah 11)

**"He will send rain to you Midrar."** Ibn Kathir glosses *midrār* as **continuous rain**. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said, "It means some of it following others" — shower after shower, one on the heels of the last. The surah's own translation renders it as an abundant shower. The picture is not a single downpour, but a sky that keeps opening.

### And what comes with it (ayah 12)

*"And give you increase in wealth and children, and bestow on you gardens and bestow on you rivers."*

Ibn Kathir unfolds it as a chain: Allah "will increase your provisions for you and provide you with water from the blessings of the sky. He will cause the blessings of the earth and crops to grow for you. He will increase your livestock animals for you and give you more wealth and children… and gardens with various types of fruits. He will cause rivers to flow among these gardens."

Follow the order he gives. Water comes down; the earth's blessings and crops come up; livestock increase; wealth grows; households grow; orchards bear many kinds of fruit; and rivers run among them. The sequence itself is a picture of provision building on provision — moving from a cloud to a garden with a river through it. And in Ibn Kathir's reading, the whole chain hangs off one condition: repent, seek forgiveness, obey.

## A note on what forgiveness covers

Earlier in this same call, at ayah 4, Nuh tells his people that Allah "will forgive you **of** your sins" — in Arabic, *yaghfir lakum **min** dhunūbikum*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on that little word *min*, and the point it makes is worth carrying into ayah 10.

**View one — *min* divides into parts** (it means "some of"). On this reading, what embracing faith forgives are the sins that pertain to the Divine rights. Sins that violate **the rights of other human beings** are forgiven only when the believer fulfils those rights — for instance financial obligations; and where the wrong cannot be undone, such as hurting somebody physically or verbally, "the person who has been so hurt must first be requested to forgive."

**View two — *min* is *zāʾidah***, carrying no meaning of its own and added only because of usage. On this reading, all their sins would be forgiven.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that even on the second reading, on the basis of other texts this general expression is subject to the conditions just mentioned — and that the report that embracing faith forgives all sins must be understood in the same light.

**Why this matters practically:** seeking Allah's forgiveness (*istighfār*) is real and it is powerful, but on this reading it is not a way of walking around the people you have wronged. If your sin has a victim, part of turning back is going to that person — settling what is owed, or asking them to pardon you.

## From the Companions: ʿUmar and the prayer for rain

Because of ayah 11, Ibn Kathir notes, **it is recommended to recite this surah in the prayer for rain**.

And he reports this from the Commander of the Faithful, **ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab**. ʿUmar ascended the Minbar to perform the prayer for rain — and *"he did not do more than seeking Allah's forgiveness and reciting the Ayat that mention seeking Allah's forgiveness,"* among them this very passage: *"Ask forgiveness from your Lord, verily He is Oft-Forgiving; He will send rain to you Midrar."*

Then ʿUmar said: **"Verily, I have sought rain with the keys of the sky which cause the rain to descend."**

He gave them *istighfār*, and named it the keys that open the sky. He had taken ayah 11 as a working promise, not a piece of ancient history.

## What comes next: encouragement, then a counterweight

One more thing, and it belongs to the ayah after ours — but Ibn Kathir attaches it directly to what we have just read, so it should not be left out.

Having laid out the gardens and the rivers, he says: **"This is the position of the invitation with encouragement. Then He made it balanced for them by using intimidation."** Ayat 10–12, in other words, are the drawing-in half of the appeal — and they were never meant to stand alone. Immediately after, ayah 13 asks: *"What is the matter with you, that you do not hope for any **Waqar** from Allah?"* — meaning **great majesty**, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ad-Dahhak all said. Ibn ʿAbbas explained it: "That you all do not magnify Allah in the proper manner that He deserves to be magnified. Meaning, you do not fear His punishment and His vengeance."

So the promise of gardens is not the whole picture, and Ibn Kathir will not let it be read as though it were.

## Living it

**Take seeking forgiveness seriously as a cause, not only a comfort.** Ibn Kathir spells out the condition attached to ayat 11–12: repent, seek His forgiveness, obey Him — and provision follows. ʿUmar, seeking rain, did exactly that and called it the keys of the sky.

**But keep it honest.** "Return to Him and turn away from what you are involved in" — Ibn Kathir's words. Seeking forgiveness while staying in the sin is not what the ayah is asking for. And per Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, if people have been wronged, settle with them; that part is not covered by words alone.

**Do not despair of the size of your sin.** Nuh was speaking to people who had spent centuries in shirk, and he still told them their Lord is *Ghaffār* — He will accept repentance no matter what the sin is, even disbelief and polytheism. If that door was open to them, it is open to you.

**Do not reduce the passage to worldly gain, either.** Ibn Kathir is clear that this is the encouraging half of a balanced appeal, and that ayah 13 answers it with the question of whether we hold Allah in the majesty He deserves. The rain and the gardens are how Nuh drew his people — but the One he was drawing them to is the point.

passages.title: Signs in creation proving Allah's majesty
passages.tafsir:
**In these eight ayat, Nuh (peace be upon him) stops pleading and starts arguing.** Having promised his people that seeking forgiveness would open the sky with rain and fill their lives with wealth, children, gardens and rivers (ayat 10–12), he now turns and asks them a question they cannot answer — and then walks them, step by step, through the evidence: their own bodies, the sky above them, the earth beneath them, and the grave that waits for them. What holds ayat 13–20 together is a single argument: *the One who made all of this is not someone you can afford to treat lightly.*

## Where we are in the speech

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. Allah is telling us about His servant and Messenger Nuh, who **complained to his Lord** about the response he had received from his people, and about how patient he had been with them over an enormous stretch of time — which Ibn Kathir gives as nine hundred and fifty years. Nuh had exhausted every method: he called them night and day, openly among the people, with open speech and a raised voice, and privately in one-to-one discussion. Ibn Kathir's summary is worth pausing on: **"So he tried various types of propagation to be more effective with them."** And still, "the more I called them to come to the truth, the more they fled from it and avoided it."

So Nuh held out the encouragement first — ask forgiveness of your Lord, and He will send rain, wealth, children, gardens and rivers. Then Ibn Kathir names the rhetorical turn exactly: *"This is the position of the invitation with encouragement. Then He made it balanced for them by using intimidation."* Ayah 13 is where the balance tips. Nuh has shown them the reward; now he shows them the One they are dealing with.

## Ayah 13 — the question that turns everything

> **مَّا لَكُمْ لَا تَرْجُونَ لِلَّهِ وَقَارًا**
> *What is the matter with you that you are not in awe of the Majesty*

The phrasing is a rebuke shaped as bewilderment: *what is wrong with you?* Notice that the two renderings in front of you differ slightly — the translation says "not in awe of the Majesty," while Ibn Kathir's text renders it "that you do not hope for any *Waqar* from Allah." Both are pointing at the same failure, and the key is the word **waqār**.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ad-Dahhak all explained *waqār* here as **great majesty**. Ibn 'Abbas then gave the sentence its edge: *"That you all do not magnify Allah in the proper manner that He deserves to be magnified. Meaning, you do not fear His punishment and His vengeance."*

So the charge is not that they were unaware Allah exists. The charge is that they held Him **too lightly** — that they gave Him a place in their reckoning far smaller than the place He actually occupies in reality. That is a diagnosis worth sitting with, because it is not a sin of the tongue or the limbs. It is a sin of proportion, and it is entirely possible in a person who prays.

What follows in ayat 14–20 is Nuh's answer to his own question. If you want to know how much weight Allah deserves in your soul, he says, *look*.

## Ayah 14 — the evidence starts with your own body

> **وَقَدْ خَلَقَكُمْ أَطْوَارًا** — *when He truly created you in stages ˹of development˺?*

The word rendered "stages" is **aṭwār**. Ibn Kathir reports that this has been explained as the sequence in the womb: **from a drop of sperm, then from a hanging clot, then from a lump of flesh** — and he names six early authorities who said this: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, Yahya bin Rafi', As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The argument is beautifully placed. Before pointing at the sky, Nuh points at *them*. Every person he is addressing was moved through those stages by a power that was not their own, that they never consented to, and that they cannot remember. You did not build yourself. The nearest thing to you is already an argument against your indifference.

## Ayat 15–16 — now look up

> **أَلَمْ تَرَوْا كَيْفَ خَلَقَ اللَّهُ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ طِبَاقًا** — *See you not how Allah has created the seven heavens in tiers?*

**Ṭibāqan**, Ibn Kathir explains, means **one above another** — layered, each above the next.

Ibn Kathir does something instructive here. He raises the question of whether this is a matter comprehended simply by hearing it, or one of those matters perceived with the senses — the sort of thing known from the movements of the heavenly bodies and the eclipses — and then he deliberately declines to go there: *"It is known that they (the scholars) have many different opinions about these matters that we will not discuss here."* The only intent here, he says, is the ayah's own point: that Allah created the seven heavens in tiers. That restraint is itself a lesson. Nuh's point does not depend on winning an astronomical debate; it depends on the sheer fact of a made, ordered, layered sky above a creature who made none of it.

> **وَجَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ فِيهِنَّ نُورًا وَجَعَلَ الشَّمْسَ سِرَاجًا** — *And has made the moon a light therein, and made the sun a lamp.*

Then ayah 16 draws a distinction the Arabic makes carefully. The moon is placed as **nūr** (a light); the sun is made **sirāj** (a lamp). Ibn Kathir: *"He made a distinction between them (the sun and moon) in reference to their lighting. He made each one of them in a set manner with a distinct quality so that the night and day may be known."* Day and night are known by the rising and setting of the sun. And for the moon, Allah "determined fixed stations and positions," and made its light vary — increasing until it reaches a maximum, then decreasing until it is completely veiled — and this, Ibn Kathir says, shows the passing of months and years. He cites the parallel verse: *"It is He Who made the sun a shining thing and the moon as a light and measured out for its stages that you might know the number of years and the reckoning"* (10:5).

So the sky is not merely beautiful. It is a **calendar and a clock**, hung above every human being who ever lived. The one who reads it can date his life; the one who ignores it still lives by it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose of these two ayat plainly: they are **"adduced as proof positive of Divine Oneness and His power."** Maʿārif also notes a fine point of wording — the prepositional phrase in the verse ("and has made the moon a light **therein**," *fīhinna*) *apparently* indicates that the moon is placed in the body of the heavens — and refers the reader to its fuller treatment of the same subject in Surah Al-Furqan, under the verse: *"Glorious is the One who made stellar formations in the sky and placed therein a lamp (sun) and a bright moon"* (25:61). Note the word "apparently": Maʿārif is reading the surface of the expression and flagging it as such, not laying down a settled cosmology.

## Ayat 17–18 — out of the earth, back into it, out again

> **وَاللَّهُ أَنبَتَكُم مِّنَ الْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا** — *Allah ˹alone˺ caused you to grow from the earth like a plant.*

Here the Arabic itself carries an emphasis, and Ibn Kathir's remark on it is short and admiring: this (*nabāt*) **is a verbal noun for emphasis, and "its usage here is most excellent."** The image is worth noticing too. Human beings are not described here as manufactured or assembled, but as *grown* from the earth — the same way a plant is brought out of the ground.

That image then does something the disbelievers had not bargained for. Ayah 18 completes the arc in two beats: **"Then He will return you to it"** — Ibn Kathir: *when you die* — **"and then simply bring you forth."** Ibn Kathir: *"on the Day of Judgement He will repeat your creation just as He first originated you."*

This is the hinge of the whole passage. Nuh's people were being offered rain, wealth, children and gardens — all of it in this world. Ayah 18 tells them the ledger does not close at the graveside. The same soil that received them will hand them back. And note the shape of Ibn Kathir's phrase: the second bringing-forth is a *repetition* of the first, not some different and harder kind of act. The One who brought you out of the earth once will do it again.

## Ayat 19–20 — the earth under your feet

> **وَاللَّهُ جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ بِسَاطًا** — *And Allah ˹alone˺ spread out the earth for you*

Ibn Kathir's rendering is "made for you the earth a wide expanse," and he unpacks the word **bisāṭ** with four verbs: *"He spread it out, leveled it, settled it, and stabilized it with firm and lofty mountains."* Four actions for one favour — and the mountains are named as part of what makes the ground steady enough to live on.

> **لِّتَسْلُكُوا مِنْهَا سُبُلًا فِجَاجًا** — *to walk along its spacious pathways.*

And the purpose clause in ayah 20, in Ibn Kathir's words: *"He created it so that you may settle in it and travel in it wherever you wish, from its different sides, areas and regions."*

Notice the little word "for you" (*lakum*) in ayah 19. The earth is not merely spread; it is spread **for you**. Every road you have ever driven, every field anyone has ever farmed, exists because the ground was made walkable on purpose.

## What Nuh is driving at

Ibn Kathir closes this passage by naming the conclusion the whole argument is built to force:

All of this is what Nuh informed them of concerning **Allah's power and His greatness** in creating the heavens and the earth. It demonstrates the favour He did for them by making both heavenly benefits and earthly benefits. For He is the Creator and the Sustainer, who made the heaven a building and the earth a bed, and who enlarged His provisions for His creatures. **Therefore He is the One whom it is obligatory to worship, and to accept as One.** No one should be associated with Him as a partner, because — in Ibn Kathir's words — He has no equal, peer, rival, coequal, mate, son, minister or advisor; rather He is the Most High, the Most Great.

That is the shape of the argument in one line: **the Provider is the Creator, and the Creator alone is worthy of worship.** Nuh is not offering his people a new deity to add to their existing ones. He is showing them that everything they already depend on came from a single Hand, and that dividing worship after that is simply incoherent.

## Living it

**First, examine your sense of proportion.** Ibn 'Abbas defined the failure in ayah 13 as not magnifying Allah "in the proper manner that He deserves to be magnified." That is a question to ask of yourself, not only of ancient disbelievers: does Allah occupy in my daily reckoning anything close to the place He occupies in reality? Ayat 14–20 are the prescribed cure — Nuh treats a shrunken sense of Allah's majesty by directing attention to what Allah has made. The remedy is not more information. It is *looking*: at your own formation, at the sky at night, at the ground you stand on.

**Second, take seriously the link between seeking forgiveness and being provided for.** This is the promise that ayah 13 is defending. Ibn Kathir notes that because of ayah 11 it is recommended to recite this surah in the prayer for rain, and he reports this from the Commander of the faithful, 'Umar bin Al-Khattab, who ascended the Minbar to perform the prayer for rain and **did no more than seek Allah's forgiveness and recite the ayat that mention seeking Allah's forgiveness** — after which he said: *"Verily, I have sought rain with the keys of the sky which cause the rain to descend."* Istighfār, in 'Umar's phrase, is a key.

**Third, remember ayah 18 when the promises of ayat 10–12 tempt you to stop at this world.** Wealth, children, gardens and rivers are real gifts from a generous Lord, and Nuh puts them forward without embarrassment. But the passage refuses to let them be the whole story: you will be returned to the earth, and you will be brought out of it again. Living with that second exit in view is exactly what it means to give Allah His *waqār*.

passages.title: The elite's plot and the five idols
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** After many centuries of calling his people in every way he could — sometimes by encouragement, sometimes by intimidating warning — Nuh (peace be upon him) turns to Allah with a report. Ayat 21–24 are that report: what his people did (21), how their leaders worked (22), the five names they clung to (23), and how far the damage spread (24) — ending in a prayer that Allah grant the wrongdoers no increase save error.

What holds the four ayat together is a single movement: a prophet who has exhausted his arguments with people, laying the whole case before the One who already knows it. And running through it is one repeated Arabic root — *z-y-d*, "to increase". Their wealth and children **increased** them in nothing but loss (ayah 21); so Nuh (peace be upon him) asks that the wrongdoers be **increased** in nothing but error (ayah 24). The prayer is shaped out of the diagnosis.

## Ayah 21 — a complaint laid before the All-Knowing

Ibn Kathir opens by noting something easy to skip past: Nuh (peace be upon him) turns to Allah "to inform Allah — the All Knowing from Whom nothing escapes." Nothing in this report is news to Allah. So the complaint is not information-giving; it is a servant unburdening himself before his Lord, and the address that begins it — *Rabbi*, "My Lord" — carries that.

He tells Allah, as Ibn Kathir summarises, that he had presented the clear call and the comprehensive invitation in various ways: "sometimes by encouragement and sometimes by intimidating warnings. Yet, they disobeyed him, opposed him, denied him and followed the children of the world."

**"The children of the world."** That is Ibn Kathir's phrase for the class of people the masses attached themselves to instead: men "heedless of the command of Allah" who "possessed delights of wealth and children." Notice how the ayah describes them — not by name, not by argument, but by what they had: **wealth and children**. That was the whole credential. The people did not weigh Nuh's evidence against theirs; they followed the ones who looked successful.

**And the ayah takes that credential apart in the same breath:** *whose wealth and children give him no increase but loss.* Ibn Kathir's comment is the heart of it — those worldly benefits "were also for gradual punishment and temporary respite, not for honor or blessing." Wealth and children arriving in the hands of a man in rebellion against Allah are not a signal that Allah is pleased with him. The ledger, as the ayah puts it, runs one way only: *illā khasāran* — "nothing but loss."

Note too that the Arabic is singular — *man lam yazidhu*, "one whose wealth and children..." — and Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps that singular. A single figure is being pictured, not a crowd: the successful man everybody wants to be.

## Ayah 22 — what kind of plot this was

*Wa makarū makran kubbāran.* The Arabic doubles the root — literally "they plotted a plotting" — and then qualifies it with *kubbār*, which Ibn Kathir renders "a mighty plot" and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān "an enormous plan."

Two dimensions of that plot appear in the sources.

**The outward pressure.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes plainly that "they rejected the message and persecuted Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him). In addition, they let loose hooligans and hoodlums on him." Hooligans set loose on a prophet: intimidation in place of argument.

**The inward deception — and this is the part Ibn Kathir dwells on.** The plot was not aimed only at Nuh (peace be upon him); it was aimed at their own followers. Ibn Kathir: "they plotted a deceptive plot for their followers tricking them into believing that they were following the truth and correct guidance." The leadership did not merely disbelieve. It manufactured a version of events in which *they* were the guided ones — and sold it to the people beneath them.

The Qur'an itself shows the day that deception is finally named. Ibn Kathir cites the exchange that will take place on the Day of Judgement, when the followers turn on the leaders they once trusted: *"Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day: when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him!"* (34:33). "By night and day" — relentless, round-the-clock. The followers will remember exactly what was done to them, and will say it aloud.

## Ayah 23 — the five names, and how idolatry began

*"You shall not leave your gods, nor shall you leave Wadd, nor Suwāʿ, nor Yaghūth, and Yaʿūq and Nasr."*

The prohibition is issued twice over: first the general order — do not abandon *your gods* — then the five named individually. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the doubling: the people "had many idols, the five mentioned in the verse under comment being the most popular because of the deep love they had for them." These five were the emotional centre of the whole system, so they get named.

Ibn Kathir states simply: "These are the names of their idols which they used to worship besides Allah." But the sources then tell a story about *where such idols come from*, and the commentators treat it at length.

### The report Al-Bukhari records from Ibn 'Abbas

Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that these five "were all named after righteous men from the people of Nuh." When those righteous men died, Shaytan inspired the people "to erect statues in honor of them at their gathering places where they used to come and sit, and to name these statues after these men." They did so. Ibn 'Abbas is precise about what happened next: **"these statues were not worshipped until after those people (the ones who built them) had died and the knowledge was lost. Then, those statues were later worshipped."**

Ibn Kathir notes this was "similarly reported from 'Ikrimah, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq," and that 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "These are statues that were worshipped in the time of Nuh."

### A second telling, recorded by Ibn Jarir

Ibn Jarir recorded from Muhammad bin Qays, concerning Yaghūth, Yaʿūq and Nasr, that "they were righteous people between the time of Adam and Nuh (peace be upon them), and they had followers who used to adhere to their guidance." When they died, those followers said: *"If we make images of them, it will increase our desire to perform worship when we remember them."* So they made the images.

Then, in the words of the report: "When those people died and other people came after them, Iblis approached them and said, 'They (your predecessors) used to worship these statues and they were granted rain by their worship of them.' Thus, they worshipped them."

### The same account in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, from Imam Baghawi

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Imam Baghawi that the five were "righteous servants of Allah who lived in the intervening period between Prophets Adam and Nuh (peace be upon them)," widely revered, whose footsteps people followed even after their deaths while still complying with Allah's injunctions. Then Shaytan misled them: he put it to them that if they made pictures of their righteous elders and placed them in front, "their worship would be perfect and they would attain the quality of humility and humbleness." They carved the statues and placed them in their temples; seeing them refreshed their memories and stirred a special feeling. "That generation gradually died and a new generation came up. Satan played another trick with them. He imparted to them that the object of worship of their elders were statues and idols. They fell for this trick and worshipped them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: **"This is the beginning of idol-worship or idolatry."** And from there, "People of Prophet Nuh (peace be upon him) gradually got steeped in idolatry."

### What these reports are teaching

Line up the three tellings and a common mechanism appears, worth sitting with:

- **It started with love for the righteous, not hatred of religion.** In none of these accounts does the first generation intend shirk (associating partners with Allah). The stated motive is devotional — *it will increase our desire to perform worship*; *their worship would be perfect* and humble.
- **The first generation did not worship the statues.** Ibn 'Abbas is explicit on this. They knew exactly what a statue was.
- **The corruption arrived when the knowledge died.** "Until after those people had died and the knowledge was lost." Nobody present witnessed the change; a later generation simply inherited the result.
- **In every one of these reports, the ruin lands only after the first generation is gone.** Ibn 'Abbas: after "those people had died". Muhammad bin Qays: "when those people died and other people came after them". Imam Baghawi: "that generation gradually died and a new generation came up." The people who built the images were not the people who bowed to them.
- **The final lie was a lie about provision.** Iblis told them their predecessors "were granted rain by their worship of them" — attributing to carved stone what belongs to Allah alone.

### Where the five idols ended up

Ibn Kathir, reporting from Ibn 'Abbas in Al-Bukhari, traces them into Arab history — the same names, still being worshipped long afterwards, for "the idols that were among the people of Nuh wound up among the Arabs afterwards":

- **Wadd** — the idol of the people of Kalb, in the area of Dawmat Al-Jandal
- **Suwāʿ** — the idol of the people of Hudhayl
- **Yaghūth** — the idol of the people of Murad, then of Bani Ghutayf at Al-Juruf in the area of Sabaʾ
- **Yaʿūq** — the idol of the people of Hamdan
- **Nasr** — the idol of the people of Himyar, for the family of Dhu Kalāʿ

Those were Arab tribes, named and known. The stones they had inherited were the wreckage of Nuh's drowned nation, washed up on their own shore — and this ayah tells them so.

## Ayah 24 — "they have already led many astray"

*Wa qad aḍallū kathīran.* Ibn Kathir: "by the idols that they took for worship, they mislead a large number of people. For verily, the worship of those idols continued throughout many generations until our times today, among the Arabs, the non-Arabs and all the groups of the Children of Adam."

That is the scale being reported. Not a local scandal — a corruption that outlived its inventors and spread, in Ibn Kathir's own words, through every branch of the Children of Adam.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), whom he calls Al-Khalīl: *"And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols. O my Lord! They have indeed led astray many among mankind..."* (14:35–36). Two prophets, warning of the same danger in almost the same terms: *they have led many astray*. And note what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked for — not merely that idols be destroyed, but that **he and his sons** be kept away from them. Nobody is above this.

## The prayer: "Grant no increase to the wrongdoers save error"

The passage ends with Nuh (peace be upon him) turning from report to petition: *wa lā tazidi-ẓ-ẓālimīna illā ḍalālan.*

Ibn Kathir: "This is a supplication from him (Nuh) against his people due to their rebellion, disbelief and obstinacy." He places it beside the supplication of Musa (peace be upon him) against Fir'awn and his chiefs: *"Our Lord! Destroy their wealth, and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful torment"* (10:88). And he records the outcome of both: "Verily, Allah responded to the supplication of both of these Prophets concerning their people and He drowned their nations due to their rejection of what he had come with."

**But how can a prophet — sent to guide — pray for people to be increased in misguidance?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises this objection directly, and the answer matters:

Nuh (peace be upon him) "did not invoke this curse out of despair or impatience." He invoked it only after "doing full justice to his mission for many centuries," when his people had chosen the path of deviation, rebellion, disbelief and obstinacy "and persisted in it until they had reached a point of no return." And he did not determine that point himself — **Allah informed him of it**: *"And it was revealed to Nuh that none of your people would ever believe except those who have already believed"* (11:36). That, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "made it clear to him that his people would definitely and certainly die in the state of disbelief. So he prayed for their final destiny to overtake them sooner and destroy them."

So this prayer is not a model for losing patience with people. It rests on two things no one else has: centuries of exhausted effort, and a revelation from Allah closing the file. Absent those, the door of hope stays open — as it stayed open for Nuh (peace be upon him) through centuries of calling, until Allah Himself told him it was shut.

## Carrying it away

- **Do not read wealth and status as a verdict from Allah.** Ayah 21 shows a whole nation misreading exactly that, and Ibn Kathir calls those worldly benefits *gradual punishment and temporary respite* — "not for honor or blessing."
- **Ask who you are following, and why.** The people of Nuh (peace be upon him) followed men whose visible qualification was wealth and children, and were tricked into believing "that they were following the truth and correct guidance" (ayah 22).
- **Guard the line between honouring the righteous and directing worship to them.** The catastrophe described under ayah 23 began with high regard for righteous people and an image meant to deepen worship. Love the righteous, follow their footsteps, and direct worship to Allah alone.
- **Preserve and pass on knowledge.** Ibn 'Abbas identifies the moment the statues began to be worshipped: after the builders "had died and the knowledge was lost." On this report, teaching the next generation is not optional maintenance; it is what stands between a community and idolatry it never chose.
- **Take the posture of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).** *And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols.* Ask it for yourself, and for your children.

passages.title: The drowning and Nūḥ's closing prayers
passages.tafsir:
These are the closing words of Sūrat Nūḥ. Ayah 25 delivers the verdict on a people among whom Nuh (peace be upon him) had remained for nine hundred and fifty years: because of their sins they were drowned, then made to enter a fire, with no one anywhere to come to their aid. Ayat 26–28 then take us inside the two prayers of Nuh (peace be upon him) — first the prayer that no disbeliever be left on the earth, then, in the surah's final breath, a prayer of forgiveness for himself, his parents, and every believing man and woman.

What binds the passage is that these are the two halves of one prophet's heart set side by side: a plea for the end of a people who would mislead everyone after them, and a plea for mercy on everyone who believed. Read as a unit, the verdict and the two prayers are one movement, and the surah ends not on drowning but on forgiveness.

## The verdict: "because of their sins" (ayah 25)

**The cause is named before the event.** *Mimmā khaṭīʾātihim ughriqū* — because of their sins, they were drowned. The ayah puts the reason first and the flood second; the drowning is presented as the consequence of their sins.

Ibn Kathir notes that the word has also been recited as **khaṭāyāhum**, "their errors."

**What sort of sins?** Ibn Kathir glosses the drowning as being **"for their numerous sins, rebellion, persistence in disbelief and opposition to their Messengers."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more specific about what is meant here: the sins referred to are **the unpardonable sins of *kufr* and *shirk*** — disbelief, and associating partners with Allah. That is the charge the ayah is answering.

**From water into fire.** Then comes one of the most arresting turns in the surah: *ughriqū fa-udkhilū nāran* — "they were drowned, then were made to enter a Fire." Ibn Kathir puts it in a single image: **they will be carried from the flood of the seas to the heat of the Fire.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the strangeness of that: they were drowned in water and emerged in fire — **"an opposing punishment which is not impossible for Divine power."** Water and fire are opposites, and the commentary's own answer to the difficulty is simply that Allah's power is not constrained by it.

**Which fire is meant?** Here the commentaries part slightly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that the fire named in this ayah is not the Fire of Hell but the fire of *Barzakh* — the interval of existence between this worldly life and the life of the Hereafter, usually spoken of as the period of stay in the grave — and notes that the Qur'an does speak of a fire in the realm of Barzakh. On that reading, the people of Nuh (peace be upon him) will *also* be punished in Hell-Fire in the Hereafter, after resurrection and after being held to account for their deeds; this ayah describes the earlier stage. Ibn Kathir's own wording — carried from the flood of the seas to the heat of the Fire — does not distinguish between the two.

**A creedal point drawn from this ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats ayah 25 as a Qur'anic confirmation that people are punished in the realm of Barzakh, in the grave. And it draws the companion conclusion: since the evil-doers are punished there, the righteous believers are correspondingly rewarded and blessed with favours there. It adds that the ahadith reporting reward and punishment in the grave are authentic and successively transmitted, and so abundant and so clear that the reality cannot be denied or rejected; that there is total agreement of the Ummah on the issue; and that belief in it is the mark of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jamāʿah — the mainstream body of Sunni Muslims, who hold to the way of the Prophet ﷺ and to the agreed position of the community. So this short clause is not a passing image. It is one of the places the Qur'an anchors a settled article of belief.

**No helper anywhere.** The ayah ends by closing every exit: *fa-lam yajidū lahum min dūni-llāhi anṣārā*. Ibn Kathir: **they will have no helper, assistant, or savior who can rescue them from the punishment of Allah.**

He connects it to the scene of the flood itself in Sūrah Hūd: *"This day there is no savior from the decree of Allah except him on whom He has mercy"* (11:43). Notice what that verse does — it does not say there is no rescue at all; it says there is no rescue **except** through Allah's own mercy. The only shelter from Allah is Allah.

The most sobering illustration is one Ibn Kathir gives from that same passage: Allah **"even destroyed Nuh's (biological) son from his own loins, who separated himself from his father."** The son said, *"I will betake myself to some mountain, it will save me from the water"* — and Nuh answered him with those very words about there being no savior that day, *"and waves came in between them, so he was among the drowned"* (11:43). A prophet's own son, reaching for a mountain, and the mountain was no help. Meanwhile, Ibn Kathir notes, Allah saved the people of the ship who believed with Nuh — those whom Allah had commanded him to carry. Lineage saved no one; belief did.

## The first prayer: not one left (ayat 26–27)

Ayah 25 has already told us the outcome; ayah 26 reports the prayer that preceded it. Ibn Kathir joins the two directly: **"So Allah answered his supplication and He destroyed all of those on the face of the earth who were disbelievers."**

**The word *dayyār*.** Nuh's prayer turns on one rare term: *lā tadhar ʿalā al-arḍi mina al-kāfirīna dayyārā*. Ibn Kathir explains it as **"do not leave a single one of them on the face of the earth, not even a lone individual,"** and observes that this is **a method of speaking that gives emphasis to the negation.**

The early authorities gloss the word slightly differently:

- **Ad-Dahhak:** *dayyār* means "one" — a single person.
- **As-Suddi:** *dayyār* is "the one who stays in the home."

Put the two together and you feel the force of it: not one soul left, not one dwelling still occupied.

**Why he prayed this way (ayah 27).** A prayer for a people's destruction sits uncomfortably until you hear the reasoning, and ayah 27 is Nuh giving it.

*"If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants."* Ibn Kathir: **"if You leave a single one of them they will lead your servants astray"** — and, crucially, **"this refers to those whom He will create after them."** The concern is pointed forward, at people Allah had not yet created.

*"And they will beget none but wicked disbelievers"* — *fājiran kaffārā*. Ibn Kathir splits the two words along the outward and the inward: **wicked in their deeds and disbelieving in their hearts.** *Fājir* describes the conduct; *kaffār* describes the heart underneath it.

And then the line that changes how the whole prayer reads. Ibn Kathir explains that Nuh said this **"due to what he knew about them since he remained among them for nine hundred and fifty years."** This is not a curse spoken in a bad hour. It is what a man concluded from what he knew of a people after nine and a half centuries among them.

## The second prayer: mercy as wide as faith (ayah 28)

Then the surah turns, completely. Having asked that not one disbeliever be left, Nuh asks for mercy — and he begins with himself: *Rabbi-ghfir lī*, "My Lord, forgive me."

Watch the circles widen:

1. **Himself.** A prophet — and the first words of his prayer are a request for forgiveness.
2. **His parents** — *wa li-wālidayya*.
3. **"Whoever enters my house as a believer."** Ad-Dahhak understood *baytī*, "my house," to mean **"my Masjid"** — his place of worship. Ibn Kathir does not reject that, but comments that **there is no harm in understanding the ayah according to its apparent meaning,** which would be that Nuh supplicated for every person who entered his house who was a believer. Either way, the condition is *muʾminan* — "as a believer." That qualifier is doing the work: it is faith, not the doorway, that puts a person inside this prayer. Nuh, whose own son drowned outside it, knew that better than anyone.
4. **All believing men and women** — *wa lil-muʾminīna wal-muʾmināt*. Ibn Kathir notes that this **"includes those of them who were living and those of them who were dead."**

That fourth circle is why this ayah is not only history. Ibn Kathir draws the practical conclusion directly: **for this reason it is recommended to supplicate like this**, following the example of Nuh, and following what has been reported in the narrations and in the well-known, legislated supplications. When you ask forgiveness for the believing men and the believing women, you are praying a prayer Nuh prayed before you — and, as a believer, you are inside his prayer while you say it.

**The final clause:** *wa lā tazidi-ẓ-ẓālimīna illā tabārā* — "and to the wrongdoers grant no increase but *tabār*." As-Suddi glossed *tabār* as **destruction**; Mujahid as **loss**. Ibn Kathir notes that this is meant **in both this life and in the Hereafter** — the ruin is not confined to the flood. And notice the shape of the request: not "give them nothing," but "let whatever increase comes to them be ruin." For a heart set on wrong, increase itself turns into loss.

## Living it

- **Sin has consequences that outlive the moment of sinning.** Ayah 25 refuses to separate the drowning from what came before it — and then carries the consequence past death itself. What we do does not stay in the hour we did it.
- **There is no shelter from Allah except with Allah.** The son on the mountain (11:43) is the permanent picture of every backup plan we quietly keep.
- **Care about generations you will never meet.** Nuh's argument in ayah 27 is about *"those whom He will create after them."* A believer's concern is meant to run further than his own lifetime.
- **Make your duʿāʾ wide.** Ibn Kathir turns ayah 28 into a standing recommendation: pray for yourself, for your parents, for the believers who come through your door, and for every believing man and woman, living and dead. It costs nothing, and it is the practice of a prophet.
- **Begin with *ighfir lī*.** After nine hundred and fifty years among his people, Nuh opens the surah's closing prayer by asking to be forgiven. Whatever we have done, it is not the achievement that comes first.

The surah ends here — on forgiveness sought, and a prayer wide enough to hold us in it. *And all praise and thanks are due to Allah.*
